title: Sherman's March to the Sea
intro: Major general William T. Sherman led about 62,000 Union soldiers out of Atlanta on 15 November 1864 on a march of roughly 300 miles (480 km) through Georgia. The army lived off the land and destroyed railroads, industry and civilian property as it went.
ending: The march ended with the capture of Savannah on 21 December 1864. Sherman estimated the destruction at $100 million, and a Confederate officer estimated that 10,000 liberated slaves followed the army, of whom hundreds died of hunger, disease or exposure.

stops.text: Sherman's 62,000 men, in two columns, began the march from the recently captured city. Sherman later recalled Atlanta behind him smouldering and in ruins, and the troops singing "John Brown's Body".
stops.quote: It began on November 15 with Sherman's troops leaving Atlanta, recently taken by Union forces under Sherman, and ended with the capture of the port of Savannah on December 21.

stops.text: Howard's wing, led by Kilpatrick's cavalry, marched south along the railroad. The defenders conducted a fighting retreat to Macon, and the cavalry captured two Confederate guns.
stops.quote: Howard's wing, led by Kilpatrick's cavalry, marched south along the railroad to Lovejoy's Station, which caused the defenders there to conduct a fighting retreat to Macon. The cavalry captured two Confederate guns at Lovejoy's Station

stops.text: Howard's wing met the first real resistance. After several hours of badly coordinated Confederate attacks, the Confederates retreated with about 1,100 casualties, about 600 of them prisoners, against about 100 Union casualties.
stops.quote: The first real resistance was felt by Howard's right wing at the Battle of Griswoldville on November 22.

stops.text: Governor Joseph Brown and the state legislature left in haste as Slocum's wing approached. Slocum's troops captured the city and held a mock legislative session in the capitol, jokingly voting Georgia back into the Union.
stops.quote: On November 23, Slocum's troops captured the city and held a mock legislative session in the capitol building, jokingly voting Georgia back into the Union.

stops.text: Wheeler's Confederate cavalry struck at the advance guard of Slocum's wing here. Several small actions followed along the march, among them Ball's Ferry on 24 and 25 November.
stops.quote: On November 25–26 at Sandersville, Wheeler struck at Slocum's advance guard.

stops.text: Kilpatrick's cavalry routed Wheeler's cavalry in the Battle of Waynesboro, after earlier clashes at Sylvan Grove and Buck Head Creek in which Kilpatrick had been driven back and nearly captured.
stops.quote: On December 4, Kilpatrick's cavalry routed Wheeler's at the Battle of Waynesboro.

stops.text: The army reached the outskirts of Savannah on 10 December, but Hardee had entrenched 10,000 men and flooded the rice fields. Hazen's division stormed this fort within 15 minutes, with 134 Union casualties, some caused by torpedoes, and Sherman gained contact with the Navy.
stops.quote: On December 13, William B. Hazen's division of Howard's wing stormed the fort in the Battle of Fort McAllister and captured it within 15 minutes.

stops.text: Hardee led his men across the Savannah River on a pontoon bridge on 20 December. Mayor Richard Dennis Arnold offered the city's surrender, and Geary's division of the XX Corps occupied it. Sherman then offered Savannah to Lincoln as a Christmas gift.
stops.quote: Arnold presented him with the key to the city, and Sherman's men, led by Geary's division of the XX Corps, occupied the city the same day.

notes: Years are 1864 for every dated stop: the article's first sentence gives the campaign as 15 November to 21 December 1864, but its day-and-month dates in the narrative carry no year of their own. Lovejoy's Station has no date in the article, so date and year are null; the quote has no year. The Savannah quote does not hold the date 21 December itself (the article's opening sentence does). Left out: Ebenezer Creek (the article says hundreds of African Americans drowned trying to cross it north of Savannah, with no date, and a creek is not a place for the map), Jonesboro, Gordon, Ball's Ferry, Buck Head Creek and Sylvan Grove (named in passing or creeks), Millen and Camp Lawton (never reached), Honey Hill (a separate Union force from Hilton Head, not Sherman's route), Savannah's outskirts on 10 December (folded into the Fort McAllister text). The freed people who followed the army: Confederate officer's estimate of 10,000, hundreds dying, is in the ending. Foraging and destruction are in the intro and ending (300 miles of railroad wrecked, 5,000 horses, 4,000 mules, 13,000 cattle seized, per the article).
